draft.body:
# A timetable is a promise

## Introduction

On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on. That is a small thing, but it explains why I care about this policy. A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters. Our campus should keep the evening shuttle for one more term while collecting better evidence, rather than calling a short pilot either a miracle or a failure. My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.

## Evidence

The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week. The shuttle therefore caused a 50 percent increase in student attendance. This result sounds decisive when I write it that way. Still, boardings are trips, and one rider can appear in the count several times. The two observation weeks also landed on different points in the semester. I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official. The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.

## Recommendation

I would keep the route running while checking who can actually use it. The driver I spoke with called the last stop 'the long way home,' and that phrase stayed with me. It catches something the total number of rides misses: access has a shape as well as a size. Next term, the campus could count unique consenting riders, record missed connections, and invite comments from students who never board. This is a modest recommendation. I prefer a modest claim I can explain to a big claim that disappears when someone asks how we counted.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body: The outline totals 289 words (91 + 103 + 95) against the brief's 450-word target, leaving the document roughly 160 words short. The shortfall is spread evenly across all three sections, so this is a whole-document gap rather than a single weak section. The document needs about 160 more words of development; the brief's requirements (the descriptive-vs-causal distinction in Evidence, and the limitation plus feasible next step in Recommendation) are the natural places to absorb it.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: Still, boardings are trips, and one rider can appear in the count several times.
comments.body: The critique of the causal claim rests on boardings being trips and the two weeks differing in schedule, but it does not use the memo's most direct refutations. Source 1 (Synthetic campus transport pilot memo) states "No attendance data were collected" and "The memo does not estimate the effect of the shuttle on attendance." Citing those two statements would make the descriptive-vs-causal distinction airtight and show the committee that the source itself rules out the attendance reading, rather than leaving the strongest available evidence unused.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters.
comments.body: The "also" has no antecedent: no promise is established in the preceding sentences, so the connector dangles and makes the reader search for a prior claim it attaches to. The sentence needs the "also" removed, or a prior promise it can attach to.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on.
comments.body: The pilot is named "bus pilot" here but "the evening shuttle" four sentences later in the same paragraph. The brief and title use "evening shuttle," so this opening term is the outlier. Pick one name for the pilot and use it consistently.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week.
comments.body: The memo (Synthetic campus transport pilot memo) states only that "There were 160 boardings in week A and 240 boardings in week B" and that "the pilot was not randomized"; it never says which week was the pilot week. Labeling week B "the pilot week" and week A "the earlier observation week" is an inference the source does not support (the memo calls both "observation weeks"). Verify the week labels against the memo or soften them (e.g., "the later week" / "the earlier week") so the comparison rests only on what the document states.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official.
comments.body: "makes the argument official" is unclear: the reader cannot tell what "official" means here or what a "badge" does to an argument. The sentence needs a plainer statement of the point you are actually making (that the numbers should not be used as a decorative authority marker). As written, the metaphor does the explaining for you and lands vague.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.quote: The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.
comments.body: The methods note (Synthetic rider survey methods note) says the responses "cannot establish demand across all students," not what students "needed." "Needed" is a different and stronger concept than "demand." Track the source's term so the limitation is stated as precisely as the source states it; "what every student needed" quietly widens the claim beyond what the survey's gap actually shows.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body: No new findings. The section contains no [@lyra:<ID>] markers to verify, and its content is first-person testimony plus the thesis recommendation, which the brief and plan both expect without source citation. The two minor issues already flagged (dangling "also" in comment #4; "bus pilot" vs. "evening shuttle" in comment #5) are the only problems in this section.
